column1: What is the most widely circulated borrowing allegation against President Tinubu?
column2: That he borrowed about ₦120 trillion within three years, allegedly more than several previous administrations combined.

column1: What was Nigeria's public debt in June 2023 and June 2026, in naira?
column2: About ₦87.38 trillion in June 2023 and about ₦166.79 trillion in June 2026 (DMO figures reported by Punch and Guardian).

column1: What share of Federal Government revenue went to debt servicing from January to September 2025?
column2: About 67.2%, according to BusinessDay's analysis of budget implementation.

column1: How can naira depreciation raise Nigeria's debt figure without any new borrowing?
column2: Existing foreign-currency debt converts into more naira when the naira falls, so the naira debt stock rises even with no new loans.

column1: What are Ways and Means advances?
column2: Central Bank overdrafts to the Federal Government; about ₦22.7 trillion inherited from the previous administration was formally recognised in the debt figures.

column1: What is the difference between Nigeria's debt growth in naira and in dollars from June 2023 to June 2026?
column2: In naira it nearly doubled (₦87.38tn to ₦166.79tn); in dollars it rose only from about $113.4bn to $120.9bn, according to the Presidency.

column1: What four arguments did the Presidency use on 8 November 2026 to dispute the ₦120 trillion claim?
column2: Exchange-rate revaluation of existing debt, inherited Ways and Means obligations (~₦22.7tn), debt inherited from previous administrations, and the much smaller rise in dollar terms ($113.4bn to $120.9bn).

column1: What did the Finance Minister say in July 2026 explained the rise in naira-denominated debt?
column2: Exchange-rate revaluation and the securitisation of inherited Ways and Means advances accounted for substantial increases.

column1: What is the difference between new borrowing and exchange-rate revaluation in the debt stock?
column2: New borrowing is fresh loans taken; revaluation is the higher naira value of existing foreign debt after depreciation, with no new loan involved.

column1: Why do critics ask why Nigeria still borrows after removing fuel subsidy?
column2: Nigerians were told subsidy savings would fund infrastructure and services, so continued borrowing alongside higher living costs looks like sacrifice without visible benefit.

column1: Why does foreign-currency debt become riskier when the naira depreciates?
column2: Repayments and interest cost more naira, raising debt-service costs, refinancing risk and dependence on external creditors.

column1: Why do critics say debt servicing hurts development?
column2: Revenue spent on interest and repayments is not available for healthcare, education, infrastructure and social welfare.

column1: Give an example of a transparency demand critics make about government loans.
column2: Disclosure of loan terms, interest rates, repayment periods and conditions, and whether funds go to capital projects or recurrent spending.

column1: Which opposition figure has repeatedly called the administration's borrowing fiscally irresponsible?
Give three things the government should publish to counter the debt narrative.
column2: Any three of: a breakdown of loans since May 2023; new borrowing separated from inherited debt, refinancing and revaluation; project-by-project use of funds; completed loan-financed projects; repayment schedules and interest obligations; how subsidy removal improved finances.

column1: What is the recommended core message on national debt?
column2: The issue is not only how much Nigeria owes but what it gets in return; Nigerians deserve transparency and measurable evidence that borrowed funds deliver infrastructure, opportunities and better living conditions.

column1: How do the debt narratives damage the administration's public image?
column2: They cause loss of confidence, give the opposition ammunition, deepen distrust of official explanations, fuel fear of higher taxes, and increase pressure to prove borrowing's benefits.
